questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify the producer at the base of a food web
questions.stem: A pond food web lists algae, water fleas, small fish, and a heron. Which organism is the producer in this web?

options.text: The algae, which makes its own food by photosynthesis
The water fleas, which eat algae and make their own food
options.misconception: calls a herbivore a producer because it feeds on plants

options.text: The small fish, which build tissue from eaten water fleas
options.misconception: treats any organism that grows as a producer of its own food

options.text: The heron, which hunts fish to obtain stored energy
options.misconception: confuses the top predator with the base of the food web

questions.explanation: A producer builds organic molecules from inorganic carbon using light energy, so algae qualifies. Water fleas, small fish, and the heron all obtain carbon by consuming other organisms, which makes them consumers at higher levels. Growth alone does not make a producer, since every trophic level adds tissue from food it ate.
questions.hint: Ask which organism needs no other organism as a carbon source.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: interpret the direction of arrows in a food web
questions.stem: A printed food web draws one arrow from grass to grasshopper and another from grasshopper to frog. What does each arrow represent?

options.text: Energy moving from the organism eaten to the organism eating
The route the hunted animal takes to escape its predator
options.misconception: reads the arrow as a movement path taken by the prey

options.text: The order in which the organisms were discovered and named
options.misconception: treats the diagram as a chronological record of naming

options.text: A size ranking from the smallest organism to the largest
options.misconception: assumes diagram order reflects body size of the organisms

questions.explanation: A food web arrow points from food source to consumer, marking the direction energy moves. Grass to grasshopper, then grasshopper to frog, is energy passing up two trophic levels. Reading the arrow as an escape route fails because the arrow begins at the organism being eaten, not at the one hunting.
questions.hint: Follow the energy, not the animal.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: compute energy available three trophic transfers above the producers
questions.stem: Meadow plants capture 10,000 kJ of solar energy as biomass. If about 10 percent passes to each next level, how much reaches tertiary consumers?

options.text: 10 kJ
options.misconception: counts a single ten percent step as three transfers

options.text: 100 kJ
options.misconception: stops counting at the secondary consumer level
applies ten percent once and calls it three transfers

options.text: 0.1 kJ
options.misconception: applies ten percent four times instead of three times

questions.explanation: Each transfer multiplies by 0.10. Starting at 10,000 kJ: x0.1 = 1,000 kJ for primary consumers, x0.1 = 100 kJ for secondary consumers, x0.1 = 10 kJ for tertiary consumers, which is three transfers of ten percent. Stopping at 1,000 kJ uses one transfer, and 0.1 kJ wrongly applies four.
questions.hint: Count the arrows from plants to tertiary consumers.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify where most absorbed energy goes at each trophic step
questions.stem: A plant swallows a grasshopper, yet only a small fraction of the insect becomes new plant tissue. Where does the remainder of that energy go?

options.text: It leaves as heat from respiration, movement, and waste
It is stored in plant bone and used to grow taller
options.misconception: reads new tissue growth as storage of the whole absorbed meal

options.text: It is recycled back to the sun so plants reuse the light
options.misconception: believes energy cycles back to its abiotic source repeatedly

options.text: It passes unchanged to the next predator with no loss
options.misconception: assumes energy transfers with no cost between levels

questions.explanation: Energy leaves each trophic level as heat from respiration, locomotion, and undigested waste, which is why energy pyramids taper upward. Storing energy in bone misreads growth as if the whole meal were banked, and recycling energy to the sun contradicts the one-way flow of energy through a food chain.
questions.hint: Think about the second law of thermodynamics at each step.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: state how the widths of an energy pyramid change from base to top
questions.stem: A grassland energy pyramid shows producers at the base, then herbivores, then carnivores. What must be true of its widths?

options.text: Each level is narrower because energy is lost at every transfer
Each level is wider because larger animals need more food
options.misconception: reverses the pyramid because bigger consumers eat more

options.text: All levels are equal because energy is conserved in the system
options.misconception: applies conservation of energy to total quantity at one level

options.text: The base is narrowest because plants respire most energy
options.misconception: puts the largest loss at the base instead of each step

questions.explanation: Only a fraction of energy passes upward at each step, so the width in energy must shrink from producers to top predators. Wider upper levels fail because eating more requires more energy below, not less, and equal widths contradict the measured losses to heat and waste. Conservation of energy keeps total energy constant, not each level's share.
questions.hint: Ask how much energy the level below must supply.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify the group that recycles dead organic matter
questions.stem: Dead leaves and insect bodies pile up beneath a forest canopy. Which group releases their elements back into the soil?

options.text: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria using the dead matter
Primary consumers such as caterpillars eating the living leaves
options.misconception: confuses a herbivore on fresh tissue with a detritivore

options.text: Producers such as mosses converting sunlight into stored sugar
options.misconception: assumes any soil organism works by making its own food

options.text: Secondary consumers such as frogs eating the dead insects
options.misconception: treats a predator as the main agent of nutrient return

questions.explanation: Decomposers and detritivores get energy from dead organic material, so fungi and bacteria convert leaf and insect carbon back into soil nutrients. Caterpillars eat living tissue and are consumers of fresh producers, while mosses are producers that never draw energy from dead matter as their food source.
questions.hint: Which group feeds on material that is already dead?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: describe the trophic position of an organism that eats plants and animals
questions.stem: A bear eats summer berries and also catches fish that ate the berry eaters. Which description of the bear fits best?

options.text: An omnivore feeding at two different trophic levels
A producer that stores energy efficiently in body fat
options.misconception: equates fat storage with making food from sunlight

options.text: A decomposer that feeds only on leftover carcasses
options.misconception: calls an animal eater a decomposer despite live prey

options.text: A producer that makes its own sugars from sunlight
options.misconception: claims photosynthesis for an animal that eats both plants and fish

questions.explanation: Eating both plants and animals makes the bear an omnivore, and the fish route places it one level above the berry route, so it feeds at two trophic levels. Calling it a producer fails because every carbon atom in its body came from food rather than sunlight, and decomposers use dead material rather than live prey.
questions.hint: Count the separate food chains the bear belongs to.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: recognize the curve produced by growth with no limiting factor
questions.stem: A bacterial culture doubles every twenty minutes with no ceiling, so its curve rises steeply and never flattens. Which pattern is this?

options.text: Exponential J-shaped growth with no limiting factor in effect
Logistic S-shaped growth set by a carrying capacity
options.misconception: calls an uncapped J curve logistic because it also rises

options.text: Logistic S-shaped growth reached after a long lag phase
options.misconception: borrows the S label from a curve that never flattens

options.text: Exponential J-shaped growth ending in a stable plateau
options.misconception: mixes an uncapped J shape with a limited plateau

questions.explanation: Unchecked doubling at a constant per-capita rate is exponential growth, which plots as a J. An S-shaped logistic curve requires a carrying capacity to slow growth, so it cannot appear where no limit exists. Option D pairs the J shape with a plateau, and a plateau is by definition a limit, so the two descriptions contradict each other.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything in the setup slows the growth rate.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: name the population ceiling set by available resources
questions.stem: A wildlife team finds a deer population stops growing near 900 animals. What is that number called in the standard model?

options.text: The carrying capacity, the maximum population the habitat supports
The biotic potential, the fastest possible growth rate
options.misconception: confuses a population size with a maximum growth rate

options.text: The density dependence, the crowding that slows births
options.misconception: labels the mechanism rather than the ceiling it produces

options.text: The immigration rate, the number of animals entering per year
options.misconception: reads a population size as an annual flow of arrivals

questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is the population size above which resources stop supporting further growth, so 900 deer marks that ceiling. Biotic potential is a maximum reproductive rate under ideal conditions rather than a size, and density dependence is the crowding mechanism that produces the ceiling, not the ceiling number itself.
questions.hint: Which term names a population size rather than a rate?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: classify a factor whose effect strengthens as population density rises
questions.stem: In a crowded barn, an illness spreads faster as the number of hens rises. How should that illness be classified?

options.text: Density dependent, because transmission rises with crowding
Density independent, because illness ignores population size
options.misconception: denies the crowding effect the data plainly show

options.text: Density dependent, because each hen needs identical fixed food
options.misconception: justifies density dependence with a constant per-capita need

options.text: Density independent, because no animal can control a virus
options.misconception: reads lack of human control as proof of independence

questions.explanation: A factor whose effect strengthens as population density rises is density dependent, and pathogen transmission needs close contact, so crowding amplifies it. Option B fails because illness severity here clearly does rise with density, and option D misreads the absence of deliberate control as evidence of density independence.
questions.hint: Does the same disease hit harder in a fuller barn?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: classify a factor whose severity is unrelated to crowding
questions.stem: A two-week freeze kills the same share of a grasshopper population whether it is sparse or crowded. How should that freeze be classified?

options.text: Density independent, because severity does not depend on crowding
Density dependent, because more grasshoppers means more deaths
options.misconception: judges a factor by death count rather than severity

options.text: Density dependent, because crowding always raises disease risk
options.misconception: brings in an unrelated crowding effect to force a label

options.text: Density independent, because only abiotic events can limit growth
options.misconception: adds an abiotic rule the classification does not contain

questions.explanation: A factor that acts with the same severity across densities is density independent, and a freeze is a physical event tied to weather rather than to how crowded the field is. Option D adds a rule the concept lacks, since independent factors need not be abiotic: a cull sized regardless of density would also be independent.
questions.hint: Ignore how many died and ask how hard the freeze hit.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: predict the growth pattern while resources remain effectively unlimited
questions.stem: A yeast culture holds 400 cells in a vessel with a carrying capacity of 100,000. What happens while density stays far below capacity?

options.text: It grows at a nearly constant proportional rate, near a J
It grows at a constant absolute number of cells per hour
options.misconception: confuses exponential growth with a linear increase

options.text: It grows fastest and then slows sharply within minutes
options.misconception: brings in logistic braking far from the ceiling

options.text: It stays constant because the culture is still below capacity
options.misconception: reads being under capacity as no growth at all

questions.explanation: When population sits far below carrying capacity, resources are effectively unlimited and per-capita births minus deaths holds steady, so the total rise is proportional and the curve resembles a J. A constant absolute increase is linear rather than exponential, and being under capacity does not freeze growth; only approaching capacity brakes it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the per-individual rate is falling yet.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: locate the population size at which logistic total growth is greatest
questions.stem: A population grows logistically with a carrying capacity of 500. At what population size is total growth fastest?

options.text: 250 individuals, half the carrying capacity
500 individuals, the full carrying capacity
options.misconception: places the peak where births just equal deaths

options.text: 125 individuals, one quarter of the carrying capacity
options.misconception: misapplies the midpoint as a quarter of capacity

options.text: 50 individuals, one tenth of the carrying capacity
options.misconception: guesses a small fraction instead of using K over two

questions.explanation: Total growth is the per-capita rate times population size, and the per-capita rate peaks at intermediate density, so the maximum lands at K/2 = 500/2 = 250. At K itself births equal deaths and total growth is zero, so the tempting answer of 500 is exactly where the curve is flattest.
questions.hint: Split the carrying capacity in half.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: determine population change from birth and death counts alone
questions.stem: A fish hatchery records 900 births and 1,100 deaths in a year, with no movement in or out. What happens to the population?

options.text: It falls by 200 fish, since deaths exceed births by 200
It falls by 1,200 fish, from adding deaths to births
options.misconception: adds the two flows instead of netting one against the other

options.text: It rises, because births occur every year no matter what
options.misconception: counts only the births flow and ignores recorded deaths

options.text: It holds steady, because both births and deaths are given
options.misconception: treats having both numbers as if they must cancel

questions.explanation: With no migration, net change is births minus deaths: 900 - 1,100 = -200, so the population shrinks by 200 fish. The subtraction is the whole rule; adding the two flows cannot produce a decrease of 1,200, and listing both rates does not make them equal.
questions.hint: Take the smaller flow away from the larger one.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: compute the net effect of immigration on a stable population
questions.stem: A flock of 2,000 birds gains 150 births and loses 150 deaths in a season, then 30 birds immigrate. What is the flock size afterward?

options.text: 2,030 birds
2,180 birds
options.misconception: adds the immigrants on top of the births and drops the deaths

options.text: 2,150 birds
options.misconception: subtracts the deaths from the arrivals and forgets the births

options.text: 1,970 birds
options.misconception: treats immigrants as leaving rather than entering the area

questions.explanation: Births and deaths cancel: 150 - 150 = 0, so the only change is immigration, giving 2,000 + 30 = 2,030. Adding the immigrants to births alone would ignore the 150 deaths, and reversing the sign of the migration sends the population in the wrong direction.
questions.hint: Cancel the two natural rates first, then apply movement.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: combine all four population flows into a net change
questions.stem: A colony of 2,400 bacteria logs 320 divisions, 180 deaths, 25 arrivals, and 45 departures in one hour. What is the size after that hour?

options.text: 2,520 bacteria
2,600 bacteria
options.misconception: omits the departures from the losses side

options.text: 2,500 bacteria
options.misconception: subtracts the arrivals as if they were departures

options.text: 2,480 bacteria
options.misconception: forgets to add the divisions to the starting count

questions.explanation: Count gains first: 320 divisions + 25 arrivals = 345. Count losses: 180 deaths + 45 departures = 225. Net change 345 - 225 = 120, so 2,400 + 120 = 2,520. Answering 2,600 forgets the departures, and 2,480 leaves out the arrivals entirely.
questions.hint: Total the gains, total the losses, then net them.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: multiply consumption, assimilation, and production efficiencies
questions.stem: A grasshopper consumes 50 percent of the plant it eats, assimilates 80 percent of that, and turns 25 percent of assimilated energy into new biomass. Overall production efficiency?

options.text: 10 percent
25 percent
options.misconception: uses only the production factor and drops the earlier steps

options.text: 40 percent
options.misconception: stops after two factors and skips the production step

options.text: 8 percent
options.misconception: multiplies the two losses instead of the three stages

questions.explanation: The three fractions multiply in series: 0.50 x 0.80 = 0.40, then 0.40 x 0.25 = 0.10, so 10 percent of ingested energy becomes new tissue. Answering 40 percent stops after two factors, and 25 percent uses only the production step while ignoring what was never consumed or assimilated.
questions.hint: Track 1,000 units of energy through all three stages.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: subtract producer respiration from gross production
questions.stem: A forest plot fixes 4,000 kJ of carbon dioxide into sugar and respires 1,200 kJ of it. What is the plot's net primary productivity?

options.text: 2,800 kJ per year, the sugar left after respiration
4,000 kJ per year, the total sugar fixed by photosynthesis
options.misconception: reports gross production as the net figure

options.text: 1,200 kJ per year, the sugar burned in respiration alone
options.misconception: reports the plant's own cost as the yield

options.text: 5,200 kJ per year, the total fixed plus the respired sugar
options.misconception: adds the respiration loss back onto the gross figure

questions.explanation: Net primary productivity is gross production minus the producers' own respiration: 4,000 - 1,200 = 2,800 kJ per year, which is what remains available to consumers. Gross production of 4,000 ignores the respiration cost, and adding the two totals double-counts the same sugar.
questions.hint: Subtract the plant's own running cost from its output.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: recover a lower trophic level's energy from an upper level's value
questions.stem: Secondary consumers in a pond hold 250 kJ. At 10 percent transfer efficiency, about how much did the primary consumers they ate hold?

options.text: 250 kJ
options.misconception: assumes no losses between the two levels
inverts the ten percent into a millionfold gain

options.text: 25 kJ
options.misconception: multiplies instead of dividing to go back a level

questions.explanation: Energy flows upward, so recovering the level below requires division: 250 / 0.10 = 2,500 kJ, the amount the primary consumers held. Multiplying instead, 250 x 0.10 = 25, pushes the value the wrong way, because a lower level must contain more energy than the level feeding on it.
questions.hint: Lower levels hold more energy, so undo the loss.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why a shared predator spreads an effect across many species
questions.stem: After wolves return to a valley, four separate prey species drop in the same year. Which ecosystem feature best explains that broad effect?

options.text: A food web where one predator feeds on several prey species
A food chain where each species eats exactly one other species
options.misconception: assumes a single-link chain can propagate to four prey

options.text: A single producer that supports one species at every level
options.misconception: believes one producer forces exactly one consumer per level

options.text: A community where no two species share any predator
options.misconception: expects a shared response from species that never share predators

questions.explanation: Because the wolf eats across several prey, a change in wolves propagates through many links, which is the signature of a food web. A strict one-link-per-species chain would transmit the effect to a single prey, and a community with no shared predators would show no shared response at all.
questions.hint: Count the links radiating out from the returning predator.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify a species whose effect exceeds its abundance
questions.stem: Removing sea otters from a kelp coast let urchins multiply, which stripped the kelp bare. What role had the otters been playing?

options.text: A keystone species whose effect far exceeds its numbers
A foundation species that physically built the kelp forest
options.misconception: credits the predator with the habitat-building role

options.text: A keystone species with no effect once it is removed
options.misconception: believes keystone status implies no consequence from loss

options.text: A minor species whose removal changes nothing measurable
options.misconception: dismisses a large cascading effect as negligible

questions.explanation: A keystone species has influence out of proportion to its abundance, and otter loss triggered an urchin boom that collapsed the kelp, so the otters were keystone. A foundation species modifies the physical habitat, which is the kelp's role here; the otters instead acted by controlling a consumer population.
questions.hint: Weigh the size of the effect against the size of the population.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: predict the outcome when two species share an identical niche
questions.stem: Two grass species in one plot draw on identical light, water, and soil nutrients, and mature in the same window. What does the exclusion principle predict?

options.text: One species eliminates the other, since the niches are identical
Both grow equally well, since the two species share resources
options.misconception: assumes sharing a resource divides it without competition

options.text: Both persist together, since the plot is large enough
options.misconception: credits plot area with removing niche identity

options.text: The two grasses fuse into one combined new species
options.misconception: mistakes competitive interaction for hybridization here

questions.explanation: Competitive exclusion holds that two species competing for exactly the same limiting resource cannot coexist stably; the stronger competitor eventually removes the other. Sharing a resource does not divide it, and plot size changes carrying capacity rather than niche identity, so stable coexistence requires at least one niche difference.
questions.hint: Ask whether any resource is used differently by the two.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: interpret a time lag between predator and prey peaks
questions.stem: Bay counts show hare numbers peak one full year after lynx numbers peak. Which relationship explains that one-year offset?

options.text: Predators peak first, then reduce prey, which later recovers
Prey peak first, then predators crash before the prey do
options.misconception: reverses which population leads the cycle

options.text: Both peak together because they share one food supply
options.misconception: uses a shared resource to deny any time offset

options.text: The offset shows the two populations are unrelated entirely
options.misconception: reads a lagged association as no association at all

questions.explanation: When predators peak first, heavy predation drives prey numbers down, so prey recover only after predator numbers fall, which produces a lag. If prey peaked first the offset would run the other way, and a shared food source would not by itself create a consistent one-year delay.
questions.hint: Work out which population must rise before the other falls.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: define niche and separate it from habitat and territory
questions.stem: Two warbler species both hunt insects in the same trees but catch them at different heights. What does each warbler's role represent?

options.text: A niche, the conditions and resources a species uses
A territory, the defended space a breeding pair holds
options.misconception: equates resource use with defended ground

options.text: A habitat, the place where the species is physically found
options.misconception: equates the role taken with the place occupied

options.text: A community, all the species sharing one geographic region
options.misconception: treats one species' role as the whole assemblage

questions.explanation: A niche is the full range of biotic and abiotic conditions plus the resources a species uses, so separating feeding by height partitions the niche. Habitat is only the location, which both warblers share here, and a territory is a defended space, which describes behavior rather than resource use.
questions.hint: Separate where an organism lives from how it lives.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: pick the operative limiting factor in a desert setting
questions.stem: On a coastal desert slope, annual rainfall alone sets how many shrubs, and then rodents, the hillside supports. Which factor does the limiting work here?

options.text: Water supply, an abiotic factor set by the local climate
Predator density, a biotic factor that sets the plant count
options.misconception: makes predation the cause of the vegetation limit

options.text: Soil nitrogen, a nutrient limit that the rodents create
options.misconception: puts the causal role on the consumers of the plants

options.text: Competition for space, which alone sets rainfall totals
options.misconception: credits crowding with controlling a climatic input

questions.explanation: Rainfall is an abiotic factor and the variable that caps both plant and consumer numbers, so water is the operative limit. Predator density is a consequence of prey abundance rather than its cause here, and competition for space cannot set a climatic input such as how much rain falls.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: match a life history to its growth strategy
questions.stem: A weevil species lays hundreds of eggs, parents leave none behind, and numbers rebound after each crash. Which pattern describes it?

options.text: r-selected, with high fecundity and little parental care
K-selected, with few offspring and heavy parental care
options.misconception: picks K for the wrong reason, many young and no care

options.text: K-selected, with high fecundity and no parental care at all
options.misconception: mixes the K label with the r strategy traits

options.text: r-selected, with slow maturation and very few offspring
options.misconception: attaches the r label to K-style low fecundity

K-selection tracks crowding near carrying capacity, so few offspring with heavy investment is the opposite profile, and option C borrows only the K label while describing the r strategy's traits.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: recognize a population crash following resource overshoot
questions.stem: A deer herd grows past 3,000 animals, food runs short, and the herd then falls to 1,200. What sequence does that pattern show?

options.text: Overshoot past the range's support, then a die-off back down
Logistic equilibrium reached and held steady from then on
options.misconception: calls a collapse a stable plateau at 3,000

options.text: Exponential growth limited only by the death rate alone
options.misconception: says an uncapped curve bent downward on its own

options.text: Carrying capacity rising steadily as the herd declines
options.misconception: explains a food shortage as rising food supply

questions.explanation: The herd first exceeds what the range supports and then collapses back, which is overshoot followed by die-off, not a stable equilibrium holding at 3,000. A steady rise in capacity would require the food supply itself to improve, and pure exponential growth would never bend downward on its own.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the sign of growth from a differential model
questions.stem: A model writes population change as dN/dt = (b - d)N, with b the per-capita birth rate and d the death rate. If b is 1.2 and d is 0.8?

options.text: N grows, since b minus d is a positive 0.4 per individual
N declines, since b minus d is a negative 0.4 per individual
options.misconception: calls 0.4 negative and reverses the growth sign

options.text: N grows, since b plus d is a positive 2.0 per individual
options.misconception: adds the rates as if the deaths were stillborn

options.text: N holds steady, since the two rates are multiplied together
options.misconception: misreads the model as a single product term

questions.explanation: Substituting into the bracket gives b - d = 1.2 - 0.8 = 0.4, and multiplying by a positive N keeps the sign, so dN/dt is positive and the population grows. Adding the rates would describe a case with no deaths, and multiplying them changes the model's structure rather than evaluating it.
questions.hint: Evaluate the bracket before touching the N.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain a standing-crop pattern that runs opposite the energy pyramid
questions.stem: A plankton sample shows a thin standing crop of phytoplankton yet a heavy crop of zooplankton grazing on it. Why can that happen?

options.text: Phytoplankton grow and get eaten so fast that turnover is huge
Zooplankton hold more energy per unit mass than plants do
options.misconception: claims animal tissue outstores plant tissue per gram

options.text: Phytoplankton draw extra energy from decomposers beneath them
options.misconception: invents a second energy input for photosynthesizers

options.text: Energy pyramids invert freely whenever biomass is small
options.misconception: extends biomass inversion to the energy pyramid

questions.explanation: A biomass pyramid can invert because turnover, not standing crop, sets how much energy flows: phytoplankton reproduce in hours and are grazed in hours, supporting more zooplankton biomass. The energy pyramid itself never inverts, so option D is false, and plants cannot out-produce animal tissue per unit mass.
questions.hint: Ask how fast the base is replaced, not just how much is present.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: choose the feeding arrangement that supports long-term coexistence
questions.stem: Four fish species share one lake. Which feeding arrangement is most likely to let all four persist for decades?

options.text: Each species specializes on a different part of the food supply
Each species specializes on the same abundant resource instead
options.misconception: sets four identical niches and expects coexistence

options.text: All four species depend on one abundant prey item alone
options.misconception: puts every species in direct competition for one item

options.text: One species eats the other three, keeping food plentiful
options.misconception: treats predation as a route to four-way stability

questions.explanation: Niche partitioning lowers direct competition, so splitting the food supply lets four species coexist where four identical ones could not. Sharing one abundant resource invites competitive exclusion, and a top predator that eliminates three species reduces the number present rather than adding stability.
questions.hint: Ask which arrangement removes direct competition between the four.
